In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''functor represented by a scheme''' ''X''  is a set-valued [[contravariant functor]] on the [[Category (mathematics)|category]] of [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]s such that the value of the functor at each scheme ''S'' is (up to natural [[Bijection|bijections]], or one-to-one correspondence) the set of all [[morphism of schemes|morphisms]] <math>S \to X</math>. The functor ''F'' is then said to be naturally equivalent to the '''functor of points''' of ''X''; and the scheme ''X'' is said to ''[[representable functor|represent]]'' the functor ''F'', and to ''classify'' geometric objects over ''S'' given by ''F''.<ref name="Schemes and functors">{{harvnb|Shafarevich|1994|loc=Ch. VI § 4.1.}}</ref>

A functor producing certain geometric objects over ''S'' might be represented by a scheme ''X''. For example, the functor taking ''S'' to the set of all [[line bundle]]s over ''S'' (or more precisely ''n-''dimensional [[Linear system of divisors|linear systems]]) is represented by the [[projective space]] <math>X = \mathbb{P}^{n-1}</math>. Another example is the [[Hilbert scheme]] ''X'' of a scheme ''Y'', which represents the functor sending a scheme ''S'' to the set of closed subschemes of <math>Y\times S</math> which are [[Flat morphism|flat families]] over ''S''.<ref>{{harvnb|Shafarevich|1994|loc=Ch. VI § 4.4.}}</ref> 

In some applications, it may not be possible to find a scheme that represents a given functor. This led to the notion of a [[stack (mathematics)|stack]], which is [[pseudo-functor|not quite a functor]] but can still be treated as if it were a geometric space. (A [[Hilbert scheme]] is a scheme rather than a stack, because, very roughly speaking, [[deformation theory]] is simpler for closed schemes.)

Some moduli problems are solved by giving [[formal solution]]s (as opposed to polynomial algebraic solutions) and in that case, the resulting functor is represented by a [[formal scheme]]. Such a formal scheme is then said to be [[algebraizable]] if there is a scheme that can represent the same functor, up to some isomorphisms.

== Motivation ==
{{see also|rational point#Definition}}
The notion is an analog of a [[classifying space]] in [[algebraic topology]], where each principal ''G''-bundle over a space ''S'' is (up to natural [[Isomorphism|isomorphisms]]) the pullback of the universal bundle <math>EG \to BG</math> along some map <math>S\to BG</math>. To give a principal ''G''-bundle over ''S'' is the same as to give a map (called a classifying map) from ''S'' to the classifying space <math>BG</math>.

A similar phenomenon in algebraic geometry is given by a [[linear system of divisors|linear system]]: to give a morphism from a base variety ''S'' to a projective space <math>X = \mathbb{P}^n </math> is equivalent to giving a [[basepoint-free]] linear system (or equivalently a line bundle) on ''S''. That is, the projective space ''X'' represents the functor which gives all line bundles over ''S''.

[[Yoneda's lemma]] says that a scheme ''X'' determines and is determined by its functor of points.<ref>In fact, ''X'' is determined by its ''R''-points with various rings ''R'': in the precise terms, given schemes ''X'', ''Y'', any natural transformation from the functor <math>R \mapsto X(R)</math> to the functor <math>R \mapsto Y(R)</math> determines a morphism of schemes ''X'' →''Y'' in a natural way.<!--To be more explicit, let ''x'' be a set-theoretic point of the topological space ''X'' (closed or not closed). Then by definition there is an open affine neighborhood Spec(''A'').--></ref>
<!--
The important special case is when ''R'' is a [[topological ring]]; in this case ''X''(''R'') inherits the topology of ''R'' (cf. Proposition 2.1. of [http://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/adelictop.pdf])-->

== Functor of points ==

Let ''X'' be a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]. Its ''functor of points'' is the functor<blockquote>Hom(−,''X'') : (Affine schemes)<sup>op</sup> ⟶ Sets</blockquote>sending an affine scheme ''Y'' to the set of [[morphism of schemes|scheme maps]] <math>Y \to X</math>.<ref>[https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01J5 The Stacks Project, 01J5]</ref>

A scheme is determined up to isomorphism by its functor of points. This is a stronger version of the [[Yoneda lemma]], which says that a ''X'' is determined by the map Hom(−,''X'') : Schemes<sup>op</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;Sets.

Conversely, a functor ''F'' : (Affine schemes)<sup>op</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;Sets is the functor of points of some scheme if and only if ''F'' is a sheaf with respect to the [[Grothendieck site|Zariski topology]] on (Affine schemes), and ''F'' admits an open cover by affine schemes.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20200127110057/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/a20d/7974f4aaee5b13657341f206d6d70939cd4e.pdf The functor of points, Yoneda's lemmma, moduli spaces and universal properties (Brian Osserman), Cor. 3.6]</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20240805233933/https://srs.amsi.org.au/wp-content/uploads/sites/92/2019/05/laideoliveira-researchpaper.pdf Schemes and their functors of points (Alexander Lai de Oliveira), Theorem 1]</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Points as characters ===
Let ''X'' be a scheme over the base ring ''B''. If ''x'' is a set-theoretic point of ''X'', then the [[residue field]] <math>k(x)</math> is the residue field of the [[local ring]] <math>\mathcal{O}_{X, x}</math> (i.e., the quotient by the maximal ideal). For example, if ''X'' is an affine scheme Spec(''A'') and ''x'' is a prime ideal <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>, then the residue field of ''x'' is the [[Function field (scheme theory)|function field]] of the closed subscheme <math>\operatorname{Spec}(A/\mathfrak{p})</math>.

For simplicity, suppose <math>X = \operatorname{Spec}(A)</math>. Then the inclusion of a set-theoretic point ''x'' into ''X'' corresponds to the ring homomorphism:
:<math>A \to k(x)</math>
(which is <math>A \to A_{\mathfrak{p}} \to k(\mathfrak{p})</math> if <math>x =\mathfrak{p}</math>.)<!--This homomorphism is the "evaluation" of ''f'' at ''x'' in the following sense:

See also: [[Berkovich spectrum]].-->

The above should be compared to the [[spectrum of a commutative Banach algebra]].

===Points as sections ===
By the universal property of [[fiber product]], each ''R''-point of a scheme ''X'' determines a morphism of ''R''-schemes
:<math>\operatorname{Spec}(R) \to X_R \overset{\mathrm{def}}= X \times_{\operatorname{Spec}(B)} \operatorname{Spec}(R)</math>;
i.e., a section of the projection <math>X_R \to \operatorname{Spec}(R)</math>. If ''S'' is a subset of ''X''(''R''), then one writes <math>|S| \subset X_R</math> for the set of the images of the sections determined by elements in ''S''.<ref>This seems like a standard notation; see for example {{cite web |last=Lurie |first=Jacob |title=Nonabelian Poincare Duality in Algebraic Geometry (Lecture 9) |url=http://www.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/282ynotes/LectureIX-NPD.pdf}}</ref><!--If ''S'' is a finite set and ''X'' is proper, then |''S''| is a closed subset.--><!--

(Mention [[Lang's theorem]] and a rational point of an elliptic curve.)

See also: [[level structure (algebraic geometry)]].-->

=== Spec of the ring of dual numbers ===
Let <math>D = \operatorname{Spec}(k[t]/(t^2))</math>, the Spec of the [[ring of dual numbers]] over a field ''k'' and ''X'' a scheme over ''k''. Then each <math>D \to X</math> amounts to the tangent vector to ''X'' at the point that is the image of the [[closed point]] of the map.<ref name="Schemes and functors" /> In other words, <math>X(D)</math> is the set of tangent vectors to ''X''.
<!--== Galois action ==
Any ring homorphism ''R'' →''R<nowiki>'</nowiki>'' induces the function ''X''(''R'') →''X''(''R<nowiki>'</nowiki>''). In particular, this applies to automorphisms of a field and so the Galois group ''G'' of a field extension ''K'' of ''F'' acts on the set ''X''(''F'').

(mention [[Frobenius endomorphism]])-->

== Universal object ==
{{expand section|date=December 2019}}
Let <math>F</math> be the functor represented by a scheme <math>X</math>. Under the [[isomorphism]] <math>F(X) \cong \text{Hom}(X, X)</math>, there is a unique element of <math>F(X)</math> that corresponds to the identity map <math>\text{id}_X : X \to X</math>. This unique element is known as the [[Initial and terminal objects|universal object]] or the universal family (when the objects being classified are families). The universal object acts as a template from which all other elements in <math>F(S)</math> for any scheme <math>S</math> can be derived via pullback along a [[morphism]] from <math>S</math> to <math>X</math>.<ref name="Schemes and functors" />
